forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Broxbourne Council to repay £51.65m borrowing within 12 months
news_drafts.lead: Broxbourne Council's entire £51.65m borrowing portfolio matures between April and September 2026, meaning the loans must be repaid and replaced—a concentration of debt repayment the council's treasury report describes as deliberate strategy to retain borrowing flexibility. The council's investment portfolio—money held in short-term investments to create an emergency financial cushion—has declined by £8m to £54m during the year. The available financial buffer against the borrowing has thus shrunk to £2.35m. The council generated £2.4m of investment income at a 4.25% average return during the year, according to the treasury management report, demonstrating active cash management despite the portfolio decline.

findings.headline: The council generated £2.4m of investment income at 4.25% average return despite the portfolio declining
findings.detail: From an average investment portfolio of £56.1m, the council achieved 4.25% average return, generating £2,386,414 direct income plus £2,808,721 total including cash balances. This demonstrates active cash management while investments contracted.
findings.matters: Investment income supports the capital programme and helps offset borrowing costs. The return achieved shows effective money market engagement.
findings.figures: £56.1 million average portfolio; 4.25% average return; £2,386,414 investment income; £2,808,721 total
findings.quote: The average rate of return on the Council's cash investments in the 2025/26 financial year was 4.25%, generating investment income of £2,386,414. Total investment income including interest on cash in-hand balances was £2,808,721.

findings.headline: The council's investment portfolio declined by £8 million (12.9%) during the year
findings.detail: Total investments fell from £62m at 1 April 2025 to £54m at 31 March 2026. The council attributes this to cash flow movements without elaboration. This reduces the liquidity buffer against the £51.65m borrowing position from £10.35m to £2.35m.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor liquid reserves as an indicator of financial resilience. A significant reduction in invested cash could signal capital spending, working capital changes, or cash pressure—relevant to assessing refinancing capacity.
findings.figures: £62 million opening; £54 million closing; £8 million reduction
findings.quote: Total investments stood at £54million at 31 March 2026 down from £62 million at the start of the financial year due to cash flow movements.

findings.headline: The council's entire £51.65m borrowing portfolio is due to mature and require refinancing within 12 months
findings.detail: The maturity structure table shows 100% of borrowing concentrated in the under-12-months bucket, with 0% in any longer period. Appendix D confirms all loans mature between April and September 2026. The council describes this as deliberate strategy to retain borrowing flexibility.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is a key credit metric. A council with all debt due within 12 months must refinance £51.65m within the coming year, creating material liquidity demand and exposure to interest rate movements.
findings.figures: £51.65 million total; 100% under 12 months; 0% all other maturity periods
findings.quote: Maturity Structure of Borrowing: This indicator is required as a measure of exposure to refinancing risk.

findings.headline: General Fund services overspent by £799k, only achieving balance through one-off grants and interest income
findings.detail: The Cost of Services (General Fund) overran budget by £799,306. After accounting for Sport and Leisure trading profits, the council faced a £670k shortfall. This was covered only through additional interest income (£578,787) and a National Insurance grant (£141,785), leaving a narrow £50k surplus.
findings.matters: The council's operational services ran approximately 9% over budget. The final surplus depends on interest income and discretionary grants, not on operational control. This suggests structural cost pressures or budget management challenges.
findings.figures: Cost of Services overspend £799,306; additional interest income £578,787; National Insurance grant £141,785; final surplus £50,460
findings.quote: This is offset by grant and additional interest income giving a final surplus position of £50k.

findings.headline: £468k overspend in Property Services due to business rates on empty commercial properties and lost rental income
findings.detail: The Resources directorate overspent by £387k overall, with Property Services showing an overspend of £468,247. This is driven by costs of maintaining empty commercial properties and the resulting loss of rental income that would normally offset those costs.
findings.matters: Empty commercial property holdings represent dead weight on council finances and suggest either portfolio management issues or a struggling commercial real estate market in the borough. Lost rental income reduces the council's revenue base.
findings.quote: This is mainly due to the cost of business rates for empty commercial properties and the associated loss of rental income.
